passage:
Note from Nirmala, class teacher.
At lunch, Usha and Riya quarrelled about a borrowed notebook. "You always forget!" said Usha. "You never return anything! Remember in Class Eight when you lost my geometry box? And last summer, and..." Riya crossed her arms and said, "You're always so dramatic." The voices grew, and old items came out. Neither was solving the notebook. Later I sat with Usha and asked, "What is the actual problem today?" Usha thought. "The notebook I need tomorrow." "Then you could say that: I need the notebook back tomorrow, can you bring it?" Usha nodded, and went to try.

qa.q: What was the quarrel at lunch about?
qa.a: A borrowed notebook.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling and wanting during the quarrel?
qa.a: Angry and let down, wanting the notebook back, though old grievances took over.

qa.q: What did Nirmala suggest to keep the argument solvable?
qa.a: To name the actual present problem, that Usha needs the notebook back tomorrow, and to ask for it directly.

qa.q: How might Riya have felt hearing "You never return anything"?
qa.a: Attacked and defensive, which is why Riya crossed her arms and answered with "You're always so dramatic."

grounding: A teenager in a quarrel says you always and you never and drags in old grievances, which provokes defence.

passage:
Tuesday night. I am so annoyed with myself. I told Gautam, "You never listen! You always do this, and last month you forgot my birthday, and in June you left me at the bus stop!" Gautam's face went shut like a door. He said, "Fine, you're always keeping score," and left. I didn't even mention what actually happened yesterday: he didn't answer my message about the project. That's the real thing. So tomorrow I'll say, "You didn't reply on Monday, and I felt ignored. Can we talk about how to share the project?" Just that. No old stuff. I hope it works.
Shankar

qa.q: Where did Shankar say Gautam left Shankar in June?
qa.a: At the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling as the words "You never listen" came out?
qa.a: Angry and hurt, and then annoyed about dragging in old things and missing the real issue.

qa.q: What does Shankar plan to do differently tomorrow?
qa.a: To name one specific, present thing, that Gautam did not reply on Monday and Shankar felt ignored, and ask to talk about sharing the project.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when hearing "You never listen" and a list of old mistakes?
qa.a: Attacked and defensive, so the face went shut like a door and Gautam answered with "you're always keeping score."

grounding: A teenager in a quarrel says you always and you never and drags in old grievances, which provokes defence.

passage:
Monday: Lalit and his sister Hafsa fought over the family laptop. "You ALWAYS take it! You NEVER let me use it! Just like last year when you broke my headphones and never said sorry!" Hafsa shouted back, "And you always leave your socks everywhere!" Doors slammed.
Wednesday: Their Abbu sat them down. "Lalit, what exactly do you need?" Lalit thought. "The laptop on Thursday from six to eight, for my project."
Thursday: Lalit said to Hafsa, calmly, "Can I have the laptop from six to eight today? My project's due Friday." Hafsa blinked. "Oh. Sure. I'll use it after." It took ten seconds.

qa.q: When did Lalit need the laptop?
qa.a: Thursday from six to eight, for his project.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling during Monday's fight?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated, using 'always' and 'never' and dragging in old grievances.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday that made the argument solvable?
qa.a: Lalit asked for something specific and present, the laptop from six to eight, instead of using absolutes.

qa.q: How did Hafsa respond on Monday compared to Thursday?
qa.a: On Monday she fought back with her own complaint; on Thursday she agreed easily.

grounding: Shows a teenager escalating a quarrel with 'always' and 'never' and old grievances, and a specific present request making it solvable.

passage:
"Mridul, you said 'you never listen' to your mother just now. I heard," said Rashmi bua gently. "Sit. When I was sixteen, I said that to my mother every week. 'You never trust me. You always take Didi's side. Remember in Class 6 when you...' I'd drag up everything.
Every time, she'd get defensive. 'Never? What about last Tuesday?' And we'd fight about the word 'never' instead of the real problem.
Then my Nani told me: 'Say one thing that happened today. Only today.' So next time, I said, 'Amma, when you checked my phone this morning, I felt you don't trust me.' Amma stopped. She said, 'I was worried about a message.' We actually talked.
So try it, beta. Not 'never.' Just today."

qa.q: What did young Rashmi say her mother always did?
qa.a: Took Didi's side.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel during those weekly fights?
qa.a: She felt unheard and angry, using 'never' and 'always' and dragging up old grievances.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rashmi bua's story?
qa.a: Her Nani's advice to say one thing that happened today, which let her talk about the phone check instead of fighting about 'never'.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's mother respond to the specific complaint?
qa.a: She stopped and explained she was worried about a message, so they actually talked.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how 'always' and 'never' and old grievances made fights worse, and specific present issues kept them solvable.

passage: The rain had stopped the cricket match, and Samir and Chetan were stuck under the pavilion roof with nothing to do but fight. "You always hog the batting. You never pass the ball. Just like the tournament last year when you didn't let me bowl once!" Samir shouted. Chetan went red. "That's not true! And you always sulk when you're out early!" Other boys started watching. Samir's anger was loud, but even he could hear it wasn't going anywhere. He took a breath. "Okay. Forget always. Today, you batted for twelve overs and I got two. I want to open next innings." Chetan paused. "...Fine. Today that's fair." When the rain stopped, Samir opened. They didn't mention last year again.

qa.q: How many overs did Chetan bat today?
qa.a: Twelve overs.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling at the start of the quarrel?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated, using 'always' and 'never' and bringing up last year's tournament.

qa.q: What did Samir do that made the argument solvable?
qa.a: He dropped 'always' and stated a specific present issue, twelve overs to two, with a clear request.

qa.q: How did Chetan respond to the absolute accusations?
qa.a: He went red and got defensive, firing back with his own 'always'.

grounding: Shows a teenager escalating a quarrel with absolutes and old grievances, then switching to a specific present issue that makes it solvable.

passage: In the Lajpat Nagar flat, Pema's phone blinked at four percent and the charger was missing from the socket again. She found it plugged in beside Sabina's bed. "You always take my stuff! You never ask! Just like my jacket last Diwali, and the time you read my diary—" "Always?" Sabina shot up. "I asked you on Sunday. And the diary was three years ago, Pema!" Within a minute they were shouting about who had got the window seat on every trip since Class 5. Pema stormed out to the balcony. From there she heard Sabina's voice go thick, the way it did when she was hurt. The online class started at six. Pema came back in, slower. "Okay. Not always. Today I need the charger back before six, and can you ask before you take it?" Sabina unplugged it without a word, then said, "Fine. I'll ask."

qa.q: How much charge was left on Pema's phone?
qa.a: Pema's phone blinked at four percent.

qa.q: What might Pema have felt on the balcony when Sabina's voice went thick?
qa.a: Pema probably felt a pang of guilt as the anger cooled, sensing that dragging in old grievances had hurt Sabina.

qa.q: What made Pema's second try work?
qa.a: Naming one present problem, the charger before six, and one request, to ask first, gave Sabina something she could agree to instead of something to defend against.

qa.q: How did Pema's "always" and "never" sound to Sabina?
qa.a: They sounded unfair and like an attack, since Sabina had asked on Sunday, so she defended herself and the fight spread to old seat quarrels.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose "always" and "never" plus old grievances escalate a quarrel, and who then gets somewhere by naming the specific problem of today.
